questions.enonce: What are the primary processes involved in managing raw materials within production management?
options: Defining the list of necessary raw materials, forecasting global demand, and ensuring timely availability through procurement and storage.
Scheduling production work on equipment and balancing workstation loads.
Managing physical and information flows of semi-finished and finished products.
Training the workforce and continuously improving production processes.
questions.explication: Managing raw materials consists of defining the required components, forecasting global demand to determine quantities, and ensuring availability through effective procurement and storage.

questions.enonce: Which worker category in the workshop is defined as being capable of establishing and carrying out manufacturing phases based on a process description, typically equivalent to a CAP level?
options: Specialized Worker (OS)
Professional Worker Level 1 (P1)
Professional Worker Level 2 (P2)
High Quality Worker (OHQ)
questions.explication: Professional Worker Level 2 (P2) is capable of establishing and carrying out manufacturing phases based on the description of a manufacturing process, whereas P1 performs tasks without adjusting workstations or reading plans.

questions.enonce: In the context of elementary production cycles, which cycle starts with a Customer Order and ends with the receipt of customer payment?
options: The production cycle (1)
The commercial cycle (2)
The financial cycle (3)
The procurement cycle
questions.explication: The commercial cycle (2) spans from the customer order and purchase order through to the delivery and receipt of customer payment.

questions.enonce: How does product complexity affect the probability of successful manufacturing, according to probabilistic principles discussed in the course?
options: Complexity has no impact on component availability or flaw rates.
As the number of components and technical operations increases, the overall probability of having all components available or zero flaws decreases exponentially.
Complexity increases the probability of zero flaws due to strict supervision.
It only affects the financial cycle, leaving manufacturing success unaffected.
questions.explication: Probabilistic issues show that multiplying high individual success probabilities over thousands of components or operations significantly drops the aggregate success probability (e.g., \(0.9999^{3000} = 74%\)).

questions.enonce: What is the primary difference between a production (manufacturing) tree nomenclature and a procurement (purchase) nomenclature?
options: The production tree describes the step-by-step assembly decomposition, whereas the procurement nomenclature groups and sums up identical components found across multiple places in the product structure.
The procurement nomenclature is created by the methods department while the production tree is managed entirely by suppliers.
The procurement nomenclature ignores scrap rates while the production tree accounts for them.
There is no difference; both terms are interchangeable.
questions.explication: The production tree nomenclature outlines hierarchical assembly steps, whereas the purchasing nomenclature groups identical parts across the structure by multiplying coefficients and adding quantities.

questions.enonce: How are extraction operations (such as digging or profiling) represented in the manufacturing nomenclature?
options: As a positive coefficient affecting both production and procurement.
As a negative coefficient in the manufacturing nomenclature, which has no incident on the procurement nomenclature since the initial material was already purchased.
They are completely omitted from all bills of materials.
As a multiplier equal to the scrap rate.
questions.explication: When an operation consists of extracting quantity, it appears as a negative coefficient in the manufacturing nomenclature but does not affect the procurement nomenclature.

questions.enonce: Which classification category best fits the production of paper journals and fashion items?
options: Unit production with little repetition
Small and medium series production
Large series production with repetitive processes
Continuous chemical processing
questions.explication: Paper journals and fashion items are classified under large series production because of high repetitiveness and volume.

questions.enonce: What are the main characteristics of production organized in 'islands' (workcells)?
options: Means of production are physically grouped together in a continuous line for mass production.
Means of production are grouped mostly according to a business logic, generating a discontinuous flow suitable for high-variety, flexible production.
Means of production are moved directly to the product site, like in shipbuilding.
It eliminates all intermediate inventories completely.
questions.explication: Production islands group equipment by business logic, causing discontinuous flows that offer high flexibility for high-variety products.

questions.enonce: What is a primary benefit of a Make-to-Order (MTO) production strategy?
options: Finished product inventory is completely avoided (barring cancellation clauses), and products are customized to customer requests.
Customer delivery lead time is reduced to zero.
Demand forecasting becomes entirely unnecessary.
Production equipment never experiences idle time.
questions.explication: MTO avoids finished goods stock and allows full customization, though it introduces a lead time between order and delivery.

questions.enonce: According to Joseph Orlicky's theory in the 1960s, what is the distinction between independent and dependent demand in MRP logic?
options: Independent demand comes from customers and is forecasted, while dependent demand is deduced and calculated from independent demand using product structures.
Independent demand is calculated by the MRP computer, while dependent demand is forecasted manually.
Independent demand applies only to raw materials, while dependent demand applies only to finished goods.
There is no functional distinction between the two in MRP systems.
questions.explication: Independent demand is external customer demand (forecasted), whereas dependent demand is internal component demand calculated via BOMs.

questions.enonce: In a Make-to-Stock (MTS) production system using Kanban, what triggers the production of a component at an upstream workstation?
options: A direct forecast from the marketing department.
The arrival of an empty Kanban label or container from the downstream workstation indicating consumption.
The expiration of a fixed time schedule regardless of stock levels.
A special purchase order sent by an external supplier.
questions.explication: In a Kanban pull system, production or replenishment is triggered locally by the consumption of stock and the return/transfer of an empty Kanban label.

questions.enonce: In the Kanban sizing formula \(K = \frac{D \times (TA + TB) \times (1 + X)}{Q}\), what does the variable \(X\) represent?
options: The production batch size multiplier
The hazard rate or failure rate at the upstream station
The average conveying time between stations
The daily customer demand rate
questions.explication: In the Kanban formula, \(X\) represents the hazard or safety rate at the upstream workstation to account for potential disruptions.

questions.enonce: What does the 'Orange Zone' on a Kanban board represent?
options: A critical condition where stock rupture is imminent and production is strictly mandatory.
A buffer zone that absorbs workload variations, where production is authorized if the workstation is available.
A zone indicating excess inventory where production is strictly forbidden.
The minimum order quantity level.
questions.explication: The orange zone acts as a buffer zone absorbing load variations, permitting production when the workstation is free.

questions.enonce: How does Industry 4.0 (Smart Factory) impact modern production management?
options: It increases paper usage and eliminates digital tracking.
It enables real-time monitoring of equipment, process optimization, and flexible or self-learning connected tools to react faster to market changes.
It forces companies to abandon lean manufacturing and Kanban systems entirely.
It relies exclusively on manual scheduling.
questions.explication: Industry 4.0 leverages digital technologies, real-time monitoring, and connected equipment to boost operational efficiency and personalization.

questions.enonce: Which of the following actions contributes directly to environmental added value in sustainable industrial production?
options: Increasing fossil fuel consumption to speed up assembly lines.
Improving energy efficiency, recycling raw materials, recovering energy from waste, and integrating renewable energies.
Eliminating preventative maintenance to save lubricating oils.
Outsourcing all manufacturing steps to countries with lower environmental standards.
questions.explication: Sustainable production focuses on energy efficiency, raw material recycling, waste energy recovery, and renewable energy integration.
